title: Lesson 4: Growing Deep Roots in Jesus
description: The name of this course is Growing Deep, and this is the lesson where the name comes to life. Paul says you are rooted in Jesus. The spiritual disciplines are five ordinary roots that keep drawing life from Him, and roots always grow down before fruit grows up.

blocks.text: You have met the Father who runs toward you, the Son who gave you a new identity, and the Spirit who walks with you as your Guide. Now you step into the heart of this course. The name Growing Deep is not a slogan. Before a plant grows up, it grows down. This lesson is about the roots.

blocks.alt: A close up view of the four different soils: hard path, rocky ground, thorny ground, and good soil with deep roots

blocks.title: The Sower and the Soil
blocks.text:
Jesus sat in a small boat just off the shore, and the people crowded the beach to hear Him. He told them a story about a farmer and a handful of seed.

"Listen! Behold, a sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured it. Other seed fell on rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and immediately it sprang up, since it had no depth of soil. And when the sun rose, it was scorched, and since it had no root, it withered away. Other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked it, and it yielded no grain. And other seeds fell into good soil and produced grain, growing up and increasing and yielding thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold." And he said, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear." (Mark 4:3-9)

Four soils. Same seed. Same sun. Same rain. The difference was the ground. The hard path never let the seed in. The rocky ground had no depth, so the plant sprang up fast and died faster, because there was no root. The thorny ground let the weeds win. Only the good soil let the roots go down, and the harvest was staggering.

Later, Jesus explained the story to His disciples. The seed is God's Word. The soils are the people who hear it. The rocky-ground hearers receive the Word with joy, but "they have no root in themselves" (Mark 4:17), so they last only until trouble comes. The good soil is the person who accepts the Word and lets it go deep:
But those that were sown on the good soil are the ones who hear the word and accept it and bear fruit, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.

That is why this parable works like a mirror. Which soil am I right now? Is my heart hard, shallow, crowded, or open? You cannot make yourself good soil by trying harder. But the Sower keeps sowing, and God has promised to take out a heart of stone and give a heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26). If you belong to Jesus, He has already begun that work in you.
4.1 - Which of the four soils looks most like your heart in this season?
Rooted in Him
So where do the roots go? Paul answers in one rich sentence.
Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so walk in him, rooted and built up in him and established in the faith, just as you were taught, abounding in thanksgiving.

Paul picks his words carefully. Rooted in Him. Built up in Him. Established in Him. Your roots do not go down into your own effort or your own goodness. They go down into Jesus. The Christian life is not a better version of you working harder. It is the same you sinking roots into the same Jesus, a little deeper every season.

Notice how it starts: as you received. You did not earn Christ. You received Him as a gift, by faith, and you keep walking the same way: trusting Him day after day, abounding in thanksgiving, not exhausted from striving.
Here is the one thing to carry out of this lesson: roots before fruit. You grow deep by staying rooted in Jesus, and the fruit comes from there.

The world measures a tree by what it sees above the ground. God measures it by what is happening underneath. Root work is slow, hidden, and unglamorous. But when the heat comes, it is the reason the tree is still standing.
Five Roots That Go Down Into Jesus

Spiritual disciplines are simply the roots. They are not extra credit, and they are not how you earn God's favor. We strive because we are in the family, not to earn our way into it. Five of them show up across the whole Bible. Walk the tool below and watch each root reach down, one at a time.

Prayer. Prayer is honest conversation with God, talking and listening. The Father has run toward you, and prayer is how you keep walking down the road home. Paul tells believers to keep "praying at all times in the Spirit" (Ephesians 6:18). You do not need fancy words. Start with five quiet minutes in the morning, naming where you need Him.

The Word. The Bible is God's voice to you. The Psalmist says, "I have stored up your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you" (Psalm 119:11). A small amount each day, done faithfully, will form you more than a giant amount done once in a while. Pick one Gospel and read one chapter a day.

Fellowship. You were not designed to follow Jesus alone. "Let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works, not neglecting to meet together... but encouraging one another" (Hebrews 10:24-25). Find a church where you can be known, and one or two believers you can be honest with. Roots that grow tangled with other roots are the ones that survive the storm.

Stewardship. Your time, your talents, and your treasure already belong to God. They are gifts to steward, not possessions to clutch. "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7). Stewardship is how you stop pretending you are the owner. Generosity is the soil where greed dies.

Fighting Sin. The Christian life includes a real fight against the pull of your old self. Peter says to "abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul" (1 Peter 2:11). Grace does not excuse sin. Grace kills it. You fight sin not by trying harder, but by running to Jesus faster.
Each root returns later in the series, with prayer threading through them all. This lesson is the high view, so that none of them gets quietly dropped. Paul shows what holds all five together:
I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship.
Notice the order: mercy first, then offering. Each root is a quiet "yes, Lord" said with one part of your life, offered back to the One who gave everything for you.
4.2 - Which of the five roots feels shallowest in your life right now?
Roots Before Fruit
Here is the comfort in all of this. You do not have to manufacture your own fruit. Thirty, sixty, a hundredfold: the harvest belongs to God, in His time. Your part is to stay rooted in Jesus.

No one may see how often you prayed or stayed faithful in a quiet hour. But the fruit will show: a steadiness under pressure, a kindness that outlasts a bad day, a love for people who are hard to love. In lesson 9 you will look closely at that fruit.
4.3 - If Jesus is inviting you to deepen one root over the next month, which one is it?
This Week's Practice

Before this week ends, take ten quiet minutes and score yourself one to ten on each of the five roots. The point is not to feel ashamed of low numbers. The point is to be honest about where you are starting. Then pick one root and one small daily practice for the next thirty days. Keep it small enough that you can actually do it. The point is not to be impressive. The point is to keep your roots drinking from Jesus, day after day.
Lesson 4 Review

In Jesus' parable, the good soil is the heart that hears the Word and lets it go deep. As you received Christ, so you walk in Him, rooted in Him. Roots before fruit. Prayer, the Word, fellowship, stewardship, and fighting sin do not earn His love. They keep you drawing life from Him, and the fruit comes from there.
In the next lesson, you begin three lessons on the Bible itself, because the Word is one of the deepest roots you will sink into for the rest of your life.
Closing Reflections
What is one key thing you learned from this lesson?
What is one step you are going to take this week?
